# Lithium Extraction from Geothermal Brine

Extracting lithium from geothermal brine combines renewable power generation with direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies to rapidly yield battery-grade materials [1][2]. This approach offers a significantly smaller environmental footprint than traditional evaporation ponds or hard rock mining [2][7], though it faces unique real-world scaling and operational hurdles [9].

## Underlying Chemical Process

The extraction of lithium from geothermal brine involves pumping hot fluid to the surface, passing it through a flash tank to generate electricity via steam turbines, and directing the cooled waste brine into an extraction and refinement process [1]. Direct lithium extraction techniques can take various forms, including ion exchange, adsorption, solvent extraction, membranes, or specialized electrochemical processes [3]. For example, integrated electrochemical systems utilize intercalative and capacitive electrodes within electrosorption configurations (such as ion-gel-derived or IDI systems) to selectively capture lithium ions [1]. Pilot-scale demonstrations have validated that these processes can directly yield lithium carbonate or battery-grade lithium hydroxide [1][2]. Unlike slow evaporation methods that take months, DLE processes extract lithium with high recovery efficiency in hours [2][3].

## Operating Companies and Commercial Facilities

Several companies and commercial facilities are actively developing or operating geothermal-integrated lithium extraction projects. At California's Salton Sea—where there are 11 operating geothermal power plants, mostly owned by Berkshire Hathaway's BHE Renewables—companies such as Controlled Thermal Resources (CTR) and EnergySource are developing joint geothermal-lithium facilities [5][6]. CTR operates in the Salton Sea region, has raised over $285 million in private capital alongside a SPAC merger, and has secured a commitment from General Motors to source lithium [4][5]. Additionally, startups like EnergyX are developing major DLE projects, such as the Black Giant project in Chile and facilities targeting Smackover brine regions [4].

## Environmental and Economic Challenges

Geothermal lithium extraction avoids many ecological drawbacks of conventional pyrometallurgical methods and solar evaporation, such as high water consumption, massive CO2 equivalent emissions, habitat destruction, and extensive land footprints [2][7]. Because the brine is already brought to the surface for geothermal energy generation, adding lithium extraction minimizes additional surface impacts and fossil fuel reliance for heating [7][8]. However, DLE faces its own unique challenges, including limited testing on actual brine samples, which raises questions about real-world reliability [9]. Furthermore, alterations in brine pH and temperature during extraction can cause potential environmental impacts [9], and the estimated costs of direct lithium extraction must continuously compete with traditional production methods [2].

## Projected Future Market Growth and Policy Outlook

The global direct lithium extraction market is projected to expand significantly over the next decade [10][11][12]. Depending on the specific market segment and forecasting model, the DLE market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) ranging from 13.5% to 19.6% between 2026 and 2036 [10][11]. Overall market valuations for DLE technology and services are forecasted to increase from approximately $1.5 billion–$1.6 billion in 2026 to around $5.7 billion by 2036 [11][12]. Policy and market drivers supporting this trajectory include a strategic shift toward adsorption-based DLE systems, increasing government support that treats lithium as critical industrial infrastructure, and the growing integration of lithium recovery with existing geothermal and oilfield assets [11].

## Conclusion

Geothermal lithium extraction represents an innovative intersection of renewable energy production and critical mineral mining, transforming waste brine into a valuable resource [1][2]. Driven by rapid processing times, favorable market growth projections, and a much cleaner environmental profile than traditional evaporation or hard rock methods, the sector is attracting substantial private and public investment [2][3][11]. Nevertheless, long-term success relies on successfully navigating real-world brine testing, operational complexities, and environmental safeguards [9].
